[Slide 3]
Why Do We Evaluate NLP Systems?
● Evaluation tells us how well a system is performing. 
● Users care about whether a system is useful for a task. 
● Developers care about whether a system is improving over time. 
● Evaluation supports: 
○ comparison 
○ debugging 
○ model selection 
○ scientific reporting
[Slide 4]
Benchmark Data and Gold Standards
● Performance evaluation is often based on benchmark datasets. 
● These datasets contain: 
○ inputs 
○ gold-standard labels 
○ a fixed evaluation protocol 
● Gold standards are usually created by human annotators following 
annotation guidelines. 
● Reliable evaluation depends on reliable annotation.
[Slide 7]
Inter-Annotator Agreement
● Human annotations are not always identical. 
● Different annotators may interpret a guideline differently. 
● Inter-annotator agreement measures how consistently humans label

Inter-Annotator Agreement
● Human annotations are not always identical. 
● Different annotators may interpret a guideline differently. 
● Inter-annotator agreement measures how consistently humans label 
the same data. 
● High agreement suggests the task and the guidelines are clearer and 
more reliable.
[Slide 8]
Observed Agreement: 𝑃 𝑎
● Observed agreement is the proportion of cases on which annotators 
agree. 
● Example: 
○ two annotators label 10 items 
○ they agree on 7 items 
● Then: 
○ 𝑃 𝑎 = 7/10 = 0.70
● Observed agreement does not correct for chance agreement.
[Slide 9]
Expected Agreement: 𝑃 𝑒
● Expected agreement estimates how much agreement would happen 
by chance. 
● Suppose: 
○ Annotator A assigns Positive to 6/10 items and Negative to 4/10 
○ Annotator B assigns Positive to 5/10 items and Negative to 5/10 
● Then: 
○ chance agreement on Positive = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30
○ chance agreement on Negative = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20
● So: 
○ 𝑃 𝑒 = 0.30 + 0.20 =

0.30
○ chance agreement on Negative = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20
● So: 
○ 𝑃 𝑒 = 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.50
[Slide 10]
Cohen’s Kappa
● Cohen’s Kappa corrects observed agreement for chance agreement. 
● Formula: 
○ 𝐾 =
𝑃 𝑎 −𝑃 𝑒
1−𝑃 𝑒
● Using the previous example: 
○ 𝑃 𝑎 = 0.70
○ 𝑃 𝑒 = 0.50
○ 𝐾 = 0.70 − 0.50 / 1 − 0.50 = 0.40
● Kappa is more informative than raw agreement alone.

Confusion Matrix for evaluating automated predictions 
● For automated systems, evaluation often starts with a confusion 
matrix. 
● For a positive class: 
○ TP: predicted positive, actually positive 
○ FP: predicted positive, actually negative 
○ FN: predicted negative, actually positive 
○ TN: predicted negative, actually negative 
● Many common metrics are derived from these four counts.
Positive class (Response) Negative class (Response)
Positive class (Reference) True Positives (TP) False Negatives (FN)
Negative class (Reference) False Positives (FP) True Negatives (TN)

● It is often preferred when the positive class is important and class

Worked Example: Computing F1
● Suppose a spam detector produces: 
○ TP = 18 
○ FP = 6 
○ FN = 9 
● Then: 
○ Precision = 18 / (18 + 6) = 0.75 
○ Recall = 18 / (18 + 9) = 0.67 
○ F1 = 2 × 0.75 × 0.67/ 0.75 + 0.67 ≈0.71
● This shows the full calculation from counts to F1.
[Slide 35]
When Accuracy Can Mislead
● Accuracy measures the proportion of all correct decisions. 
● Formula: 
○ 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦 = 𝑇𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 / 𝑇𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 + 𝐹𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁
● Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced datasets. 
● Example: 
○ if 95% of items are negative, always predicting negative gives 95% accuracy 
○ but recall for the positive class is 0 
● In such cases, F1 is often more informative.

[Slide 36]
Micro, Macro, and Weighted Averages
● For multi-class problems, we often report combined performance. 
● Macro average: 
○ compute the metric for each class 
○ then average across classes equally 
● Micro average: 
○ pool all TP , FP , and FN first 
○ then compute the metric once 
● Weighted average: 
○ average class-level metrics using class frequency as weights 
● The choice affects how strongly rare classes influence the final score.

[Slide 39]
What Is Open Information Extraction?
● Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) extracts relational facts from 
text without relying on a fixed predefined schema. 
● Input: 
○ raw sentences or documents 
● Output: 
○ relation tuples such as (argument, relation, argument)
● OpenIE aims to turn unstructured text into machine-readable 
knowledge.
[Slide 40]
What an OpenIE Extraction Looks Like
● Sentence: 
○ Albert

[Slide 40]
What an OpenIE Extraction Looks Like
● Sentence: 
○ Albert Einstein published the theory of relativity in 1915.
● Example extraction: 
○ (Albert Einstein; published; the theory of relativity)
○ (Albert Einstein; published in; 1915)
● OpenIE relies heavily on earlier NLP steps: 
○ POS tagging 
○ parsing 
○ entity recognition
[Slide 41]
A Short View of OpenIE Methods and Limits
● Classical methods used: 
○ patterns 
○ dependency structure 
○ clause splitting 
● Later work introduced supervised and neural approaches. 
● Common challenges include: 
○ ambiguity 
○ synonymy 
○ coreference 
○ trustworthiness of extracted facts 
● In this module, OpenIE is a compact application case rather than the 
main assessment focus.
